utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone. Your Honour, I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber and the Defence to a development with respect to Mr. Haglund. I can do that perhaps at the end of the witness's testimony. It pertains to his availability next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, or at the beginning of the next session. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, for the Prosecution, is examining you now. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Osman Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's P01373. It will appear shortly on the computer screen in front of you. And if we could have the original version. What we are seeing now is actually what has been uploaded as the translation. If we could have what's in e-court as the original, please. It's the 92 bis package. Perfect. Thank you. And if we could go to page 4 of this document. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see in front of you a copy in your own language of a witness statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 4th of December, 2004?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall providing that witness statement to Investigator Garry Selsky on that date?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see here a signature on the lower right-hand corner. Can you identify whose signature that is under the date of 26 January 2007?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: It is my signature, that of Osman Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall meeting with representatives of the ICTY on that date in 2007 to certify this 2004 witness statement so that it could be used in court without having you need to come here to testify?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have an opportunity to recently read your 2004 witness statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest before this Trial Chamber that that 2004 witness statement accurately reflects what you told the investigators at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please have the English version on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We'll just need to go to the translation. What we've done, Mr. President, is uploaded as the original statement the B/C/S version, which the witness signed in 2007, and as the English translation we've simply uploaded the actual witness statement as it was taken in 2004, which the witness also signed, but that was the English original version back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you attest that if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked back in 2004, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course they would. I stand by everything I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P01373.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received with this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just by way of background, did you also testify in Belgrade in the state court there in connection with the Prosecution of several members of the Skorpions Unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that testimony was in approximately 2006 and 2007. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to read a very brief 92 ter summary for Mr. Salkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The witness was born in Fojhari, two kilometres from Srebrenica, and during the war lived in Joseva, a village that overlooked Srebrenica. The witness was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and served as a military policeman owing to his previous experience in the JNA as an MP. He was present in Srebrenica when General Morillon came in 1993. After Srebrenica was declared a safe area, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still organised but it was not really active. He no longer served as an active MP and stayed around the house to try to take care of his family. The witness described the attack on Srebrenica that began on 6 July 1995, and the decision on 11 July that the women would go to Potocari and that the men would walk north. He further described his experiences as part of the column that formed during the night of 11 July and set out from Susnjari. He was with his father and brother-in-law, Azmir Alispahic, who was 16 years old at the time. They were ambushed at Buljim and at Kamenica. He last saw Azmir near the road they were trying to cross. The witness reached the Muslim-held area near Nezuk. And he also identified Azmir in five photographs shown to him by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Trial Chamber has your 2004 witness statement as the basis of your testimony. That was just a summary of some of the main points. I'd like to ask you a couple of follow-up questions to gain a little bit more detail about your experiences. When the war began, sir, where -- or beg your pardon, with whom exactly were you living?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I lived with my parents, my wife, my daughter, and my sister, who was 18 or 19 at the time. She was with us in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to orient the Trial Chamber a little bit, we don't need to pull out a map, but can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately where the village or the settlement in which you were living during the war was located? And let's say, for example, can you tell the Trial Chamber where in relation to the village of Bajramovici was your village or your settlement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Joseva was closer than Bajramovici. It was just above Fojhari. We could see Srebrenica from an elevation. Joseva is some two and a half kilometres from Fojhari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are Joseva and Fojhari to the north of Bajramovici, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are they to south of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement, I think you said that the settlement was on an elevation which had a view of Srebrenica. Did Srebrenica fall to the east or west of your settlement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: To the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Could you tell the Trial Chamber just a little bit about your educational background and what your trade is.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: By education I was a mining technician. I was born on the 12th of October, 1966. I completed my education in Srebrenica, which is where I was when the war broke out. At the beginning of the war, I was in Srebrenica and if there are any details that you are interested in, feel free to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just prior to the war and during the war, how were you working? How were you employed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Before the war I worked in the Sase mine in Srebrenica as a mining technician. I began working in 1987 and the war broke out in 1992. I was quite young at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just give the Trial Chamber an idea of what kind of work you do now.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Currently I am employed in a private company in Sarajevo which provides mechanical safety equipment for facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to your OTP statement, you said - and this is at page 2 of the English, page 6 of the B/C/S - that before Srebrenica was declared a safe area in 1993, you were a soldier in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you served as an MP.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also stated that after Srebrenica was declared a safe area, that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still organised but that it was not really active.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How would you describe for the Trial Chamber the strength and organisation of the Bosniak forces in the enclave after it was declared a safe area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I believe, or rather, I know that when Srebrenica was declared a safe area, what followed was that all heavy artillery had to be handed over to UNPROFOR soldiers. They arrived with a list of heavy weaponry which had been seised from their positions, and when I say "their" I mean Serb positions. Hence, all heavy artillery had to be returned. However, it remained part of the establishment. The units remained the same in terms of numerical strength, the same people remained on the list, and smaller groups of people were tasked with performing reconnaissance in order to try to preserve the military regimen. There were no civilian authorities in Srebrenica at the time and people were left to their own devices. The situation was quite chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify, what are you referring to when you speak about heavy weaponry which had been seised from Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Mortars, Howitzers, armoured vehicles; all of that had been seised from Serb positions. Finally, it was returned to the UNPROFOR base in the outskirts of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And who was it that seised all of those heavy weapons to begin with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The soldiers. Muslims seised that weaponry from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that happened during the early part of the conflict from 1992 to 1993, just to be perfectly clear?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How would you describe the nature of the command structure of the army in Srebrenica, particularly after 1993? That is, can you comment on the experience and qualifications of the military officers who commanded the various units of the armija?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: As you all probably know well, in Srebrenica there wasn't a single professional policeman throughout the war. The army that fought against the Serb army were simply the people who took up arms to defend their homes and families. We had seen the things they had done in Vukovar and we simply had to put up resistance even though we had no weapons. We didn't have a single professional officer in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how about Naser Oric who everybody hears so much about, or Zulfo Tursunovic, which the Chamber has heard testimony about, or Ramiz Becirovic? What about those gentlemen, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, the defence in Srebrenica began by the local communes organising themselves. Each local commune elected one leader, and there were five such local communes in Srebrenica. Since Naser had certain experience because he was in Milosevic's security detail, he was elected the person number one of the defence system in Srebrenica. Zulfo Tursunovic was also elected in his own area, but he passed away a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Maybe there's a translation or some other -- something going on. Did I understand you correctly to say that Mr. Becirovic had passed away a few days ago or did he pass away some other time ago?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, Ramiz Becirovic died, I'm not certain, but it must be nine or ten years now. Zulfo Tursunovic is the one who passed away a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to your knowledge did any of the -- those three individuals, Mr. Oric, Tursunovic, or Becirovic have any professional officer training?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Only Ramiz Becirovic had been a reserve military officer who had worked in the TO Staff before the war. I don't think he had any military background, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned, sir, a few moments ago that after Srebrenica was declared a safe area the armija maintained the same fighters on its rosters and still engaged in reconnaissance. Did I have that correct, first?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. There were no military activities. A lot of weaponry had been handed over, and the units preserved the manning levels. We all awaited an inspection where the end of the war would be declared so that people could see for themselves who did anything in terms of defending Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did the Bosniak fighters in the enclave completely abandon their positions after Srebrenica was declared a safe area, or did they maintain them to some extent?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: They withdrew from their positions. All positions and elevations were handed over to UN soldiers. The Serb soldiers made the best use of it. They put up their check-points as closely as possible to UN positions so as to have a clear view you of the town and to oversee the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to be clear. Is it your testimony that the Bosniak military forces in Srebrenica completely relinquished any of their positions in the enclave after it was declared a safe area, or did they maintain some form of being able to have visibility on what was going on in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't hold a single line or position once the UN soldiers arrived, until the activities in 1995 when it became clear that there was going to be an attack on Srebrenica, and then things happened the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear anything about helicopters delivering weapons, equipment, and uniforms in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but they never brought them to Srebrenica. It all came to Zepa. Which part of it, if any, reached Srebrenica, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Bosniak forces from within the enclave exiting the enclave to execute sabotage missions on Serb targets outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that, but I know people sometimes left the free territory to bring back food or livestock because there was really nothing to eat in Srebrenica. That's the only reason I am aware of why people left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you exclude the possibility that small units of Bosniak fighters were engaged to perform such sabotage activities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after demilitarisation, sir, are you aware of whether or not there were trenches that were maintained by any of the Bosniak forces in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: You have to believe me when I say that I had no occasion to go around all the defence lines and I didn't go to every corner of Srebrenica, but the lines earlier held by the Bosniak army had been taken over by the UNPROFOR, so they -- the trenches probably remained and were kept up by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand, sir, that you served as a military policeman and not as, say, a member of the regular infantry, but did you ever become aware that there were what some people considered three rings around Srebrenica; there was what the Serbs considered their ring, there was what the UN considered its ring, and there was also what the Bosniaks considered their ring which defined the zone, the three respective zones, around the safe area? Did you ever hear that? If you didn't, that's fine; I just want to find out what your level of knowledge was at the time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I know certainly after the arrival of the UNPROFOR, there was no military activity anymore except perhaps locally people stood guard, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you testified in Belgrade in the Skorpions trial -- and this is, for the Defence, this is at page 29 of the Cyrillic transcript. You testified that the Serbs carried out an attack on the Vidikovac neighbourhood and that that was considered to be a test by the VRS to see how the UN would respond. Do you recall testifying to that effect, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber anything more about what you recall about that attack: Approximately where it occurred, what year or month, if you recall, and whether there were any casualties.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I remember that very well. That was perhaps 15 days before the fall of Srebrenica. The attack started at 4.00 a.m., just before sunrise, and according to later analysis, we came to believe they had come through the tunnel that connected Srebrenica with Sase or perhaps from Zagrici, and a woman named Semsa was killed. Her house was up front. It was a volley of fire, actually, and I'm certain it was a test to see how the UNPROFOR would react and if they would react at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just have one question about your statement with respect to the actual VRS attack on the enclave in July of 1995. You say in your statement that your village was shelled on 11 July from Zalazje and Zvijezda.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where those locations are?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: It's not so easy to explain. Zalazje is east of Srebrenica and east of Joseva. In Joseva there was no activity at all the whole duration of the war and it was probably never even necessary to shell it earlier. However, on the 11th of July, the main road from Srebrenica towards Susnjari went through Joseva. It was a shorter route and a safer one. And they probably saw the column moving along that road and that's why they shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Those two locations, sir, are they within the Srebrenica Opstina, the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, inside the municipality. It was approximately the positions where the observation posts of the UN were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn your attention now to the column of men and boys that set out from Susnjari on the night of the 11th. Did you carry a weapon, sir, when you set out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: If you are asking about me personally, yes, I did have a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that you were towards the front of the column. Can you describe how well armed that portion of the column was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: For the most part those were semi-automatic and automatic rifles and if there were 3.000 men in that first group, perhaps 1.000 of them had rifles. That's one in three.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you set out, who did you set out with among your family members?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: My father and my relatives and Casmir [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the brother of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we just need you, for the sake of the record, to repeat the last name again so that we can have it clear.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Alispahic, Azmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll be asking you a few more questions about him in a moment. How old was Azmir when you set out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1978; that means he was 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about your father? Can you tell us how old he was when you all set out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: His year of birth is 1939, and that made him 52 or 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe 56 or 57, depending on how you do the math, but I think we are in the right -- we are in the right ballpark, so it's not a math test here, sir, don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: He was born in April 1939. That's when my father was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's all we need. Now, you described in your statement being shelled first at Buljim on 12 July and then being ambushed again at Kamenica later that morning. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what it was like during those ambushes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: It's very hard to describe unless you've lived through it, but I'll try, very briefly. From the time we left Srebrenica, a column formed, heading for Buljim. We were trying to decide where to go, in which direction. The first shelling where I was involved was on the 12th. I was already at Buljim, and that's where I witnessed the first shelling. And when I say "shelling," that means a lot of artillery weapons targeting flesh and blood, and who survives, survives. We survived the first shelling, and the next ambush came just before we reached Kamenica, in the area of Bratunac. Then we took a small break, forming columns to go on. However, when we were supposed to make the decision and head for the tarmac road towards Konjevic Polje, just before sun -- just before sunset, the fiercest possible shelling started and our column was bisected and the people heading for free territory became separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many days did you spend in the woods before crossing over into free territory?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that you crossed over near Nezuk. Did you pass by the VRS positions and trenches in the area of Baljkovica before reaching the free territory?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether there had been fierce fighting prior to you passing through Baljkovica between members of the column and the VRS forces at those positions in Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that, yes, there was fighting. However, we broke through the defence line so that 2.500 to 3.000 of us managed to cross over into free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, before we begin speaking a little bit more about Azmir Alispahic, you have another brother-in-law named Jusuf Ahmedovic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: He remained in another part of the column that was separated from us. He realised he couldn't pass through. He returned to Srebrenica. They made some sort of trenches, dugouts in the forest, and they managed to survive two and a half months. And then when combat activities ceased, they crossed over unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about your relationship with Azmir Alispahic. For example, how often would you see him before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I know Azmir from the second year of primary school, and when I was dating my wife, I used to see him every day. Later on, when my wife and I moved in together, or rather, she moved into my house, Azmir visited very often, so I saw him growing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And please tell the Chamber as precisely as you can remember, when was the last time you saw Azmir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was at Kamenica near Bratunac, before the fierce shelling started. He was still a child, though, he couldn't dodge the shells. He was overwhelmed by panic and he probably perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you some photographs. These are referred to in your OTP statement as photographs 9, 10, 11, 12, and 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's start with P01374, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell Trial Chamber who either of the men in this photograph are? Let's start moving from the right-hand of the screen -- or I beg your pardon, let's start from the left-hand of the screen and move to the right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The first one with his head bent, his arms crossed on his back, in a blue shirt is Sidik Salkic. And the second one is Azmir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the first man that you identified, Sidik Salkic, is he any relation to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what he did during the war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Sidik Salkic was a driver in the medical service in the health centre in Srebrenica. And I believe as they were moving, he recognised Azmir and took him under his wing to protect him. Some stories circulated that they were captured in Zvornik. And Srebrenica had links with Zvornik between health services, people came from -- people went to Zvornik to get treatment, and that's how they knew each other from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So basically this relation of yours, Sidik Salkic, drove an ambulance during the war; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "relation," "connection"?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am sorry, there may be a problem with the word I used. This man you've identified as Sidik Salkic, is it fair to say that he drove an ambulance during the war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no ambulances in Srebrenica during the war. There was not a single car in Srebrenica going around except for those little vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand. Could the witness be asked to explain the word he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we are having a hard time understanding the last word you used to describe the small vehicles. Could you just try again, please, so we can have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: When I use this term, I have to stress before the arrival of the UNPROFOR you could not drive anything in Srebrenica because there was no petrol, there was no diesel, there was no petroleum for the petroleum lamp, for the oil lamp to sit down to have dinner under the light. It was only with the arrival of the UNPROFOR that we began to get certain amounts of fuel. Second of all, not a single car was able to leave Srebrenica, but in Srebrenica itself you did not practically need cars. Everyone -- everything was done on foot or using carts, but Sidik did work as an ambulance driver as part of his work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So was that before the war, then, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at P01375, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask an additional question to clarify something. You said Mr. Sidik Salkic was a relative of yours. Could you describe your relation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say that my grandfather and his grandfather were brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'll go ahead and tender P1374 while we are getting P1375 up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you tendering the last photograph we have seen on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we are looking at the second of the five photographs you identified during your interview in December of 2004, very similar to the one we just looked at. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you identify any of the individuals in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The first one is Sidik Salkic, the second one is Azmir Alispahic. When I say "first," I mean the man looking down, with his head bent, in the white short-sleeved shirt -- in a blue short-sleeved shirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have still the first photograph on the screen, or is it quite similar to the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, they are very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the Prosecution would tender P1375, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 1376, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Azmir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, he is the only individual whose full face you can see in this image; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders P01377 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 1376, beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was jumping ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just one question while we are looking at this photograph: You said in your witness statement that when you last saw Azmir Alispahic he was wearing a white T-shirt and a black leather jacket and jeans, and we can see in the photographs that we've seen that he is not wearing a black leather jacket. He appears to be wearing a blue or green sweat shirt or top of some kind. How do you account for the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: It had been raining and they were captives. It's possible that he had lost his jacket and was looking for something dry to wear. It's also possible that they took his jacket away from him and gave him a shirt. He had proper shoes on his feet, or trainers, but when we identified his remains, we found only soles of the shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P1377, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, very similar to the last photograph, but just wanted to show you the exact photographs that are referred to in your OTP witness statement. Do you recognise the individual in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes; Azmir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders P1377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And lastly, may we have P1378.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The first person is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just repeat the name of the first person.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Sidik Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you referring to the first person on the right or on the left of the image?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: On the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone else in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Azmir Alispahic is the second person in the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again moving from right to left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Prosecution tenders P1378, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just have one final area to ask you about. You mentioned in your Belgrade testimony in the Skorpions trial - and this is at page 44 in the Cyrillic, for the Defence's benefit - that it was very painful for you when you saw people from Bratunac and they were using the word "balija" towards the Muslims. Do you remember saying that during your Belgrade testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard that the Muslims sometimes referred to the Bosnian Serbs as "Chetniks" and that the Bosnian Serbs sometimes referred to the Muslims as "Turks." Is there a difference, from your experience as a Bosniak, between using the word "Turk" and using the word "balija"? And if so, what does it tell you about the attitude of somebody who uses the word "balija"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, if someone calls you "balija," it means that you are the lowest of the low and that that person does not see you as a human being, or anything positive, for that matter. When they say a Turk, what I could say is that they probably believe that we have some Turk ancestry, Turkish ancestry. It was very difficult for us to be so humiliated, because in Srebrenica, before the war, there were exceptionally good neighbourly relations among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Sir, now, Mr. Tolimir has the right to cross-examine you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house. I would like to greet everyone present, including the witness, wishing that the hearing today and the entire proceedings should be concluded according to God's will and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since we speak the same language, we'll have to take care that we pause between questions and answers so as not to overlap and so that the interpreters could interpret everything. We will follow the line of questioning used during examination-in-chief. On page 21 and page 22 in lines 25 you explained to Mr. Thayer the difference between the terms "balija," "Turk," et cetera. We know what your answer was. You said that there were good neighbourly relations in town, but can you tell us whether the Muslims wanted to remain in this joint country, joint state, and were they invited to do so?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: General, I think you know well the statement made by Mr. Karadzic during the Assembly session in Sarajevo. You know what he said and you know who levelled threats against whom and whose existence was threatened. We know what was in store for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you referred to Karadzic. Perhaps I was unclear and I'll try to be clearer. In Serbia and from the FRY have there been invitations to the population, Muslim population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to remain part of the joint state after the secession of Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in politics, but I do know what things took place in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you know what took place, can you tell us how it came about that Bosnia-Herzegovina too seceded from the FRY? Because the Chamber knows of the SFRY before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: You know well there was a referendum and that the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina opted for independence, to have an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for you, the army, and why you did not equally defend both peoples, that is the question. Why did you allow this war to take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this correspond to the gist of what you said when you said that it was painful for you to see it all because Muslims wanted to live alongside Serbs, but now you are telling us that even before the war the Muslims asked to secede from the FRY and the Serbs by way of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I must say that there is a very strong political note to your questions. Even nowadays, after the war, we still live together, the Serbs and Muslims. In Srebrenica today no Serb touches me and I don't touch anyone else. We still live together. We do again. Perhaps you are at odds with this, but yes, we do share a common life. It is our destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I understand you. And I can't lecture you on politics like you tried to lecture us, but I'm asking you whether before the war the Muslims decided to leave the FRY, for the record.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my question, because you said that you wanted to continue living alongside the Serbs, but yet you see that Bosnia-Herzegovina held that referendum. My second question is also based on something you said. Did the Muslims first leave Srebrenica and go -- went to some other neighbouring settlements at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were those settlements, in terms of altitude, higher than Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us why they did that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Given that the population in Srebrenica mainly hailed from the periphery of the town, from the larger local communes, they went there because they could join their relatives and felt safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who left Srebrenica first, the Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "first"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was the first to leave Srebrenica, Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that anyone left anything. You know how the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina. People were afraid, that's why they left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That may well be your opinion and I won't question it. That is not my task here. Let us discuss the column you were asked about by Mr. Thayer. There was a number of questions. On page 12 of today's transcript, line 23, he asked you where your village is located, and you said that a column went through the village, heading for Susnjari, and that on that day it was shelled for the first time. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember having said that every third person in the column had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, you misheard, and I'd like to complete my answer, if I may. The question was related to the first group who went out as reconnaissance, how many of them were armed. Sir, you know very well how many people crossed over in the first group to the free territory in Tuzla. You know how many were captured. You know well who handed in their weapons and who searched the terrain. All of that terrain was under the control of the VRS, and I had occasion to speak to some top officials from the VRS who disagreed with what took place in the area, and you know well what took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who did you have those discussions with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I'd rather not go into that because of their safety or the safety of that person. Most of the people who were in the Serb army in Srebrenica yelled out to our positions from theirs. They communicated with us. I know that you will dispute that because you tried to impose the regimen of standing at attention, but I know that people were actually doing that. They still live in Srebrenica, and I have the Serbs in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a court. If you believe that there is something you shouldn't say in open session, please do not say that because we cannot use that any further. If you want to tell us the name of that person, you can tell us in closed session.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Why should I refer to his name when he doesn't want his name to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please be asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters ask not to overlap because you are both speakers speeding up and I have to interrupt you that we didn't receive any more interpretation. Please repeat your last question, and then don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to you and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 13 of today's transcript, line 15, the witness said that he had a hunting rifle. Actually, it is lines 14 and 15. Then he said that 1.000 pieces of weapons were carried over, each and every person had at least some weapon. That was in lines 14 and 15. My question hence is this: If every third person in that part of the column you referred to had a weapon, does this make the column a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the military parlance and I don't know what a military target is. I can tell you what the situation was, and then you are there to explain what it is that you targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when the column was formed and when it left Susnjari and the other villages surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: There was no official time it was formed. As people were leaving the town and as were being driven out of those parts of the town closest to the Serbs -- I don't know if you are following?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The column was formed spontaneously as people were withdrawing in front of the advancing troops. That is why the column was formed, and the women and children left the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the women and children were headed for Potocari and did you arrange with that part of the population that you were to leave for Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I would always take the forest route and I believe that it was safer for the women and children to go down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So before you left for Susnjari you knew that the women and children would go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After the break - because we only have four minutes left - we will see some footage, but for now, can you tell us whether, since you moved in that column for six days, were there any women in the column?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were an active member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell us whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica had women in its ranks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that, but definitely not. They didn't carry weapons and there weren't enough pieces to go around for the men, let alone women.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D05 for the witness to peruse it. Actually, it is 1D105. Thank you, Aleksandar. I wasn't clear about the number. 1D105.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, I'll give a background. This is a document of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Srebrenica, sent by the secretary, Professor Suljo Hasanovic, from Srebrenica on the 1st of February, 1995. Do you know Suljo Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I do, but I don't know how this was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he have anything to do with the municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he worked in the secretariat, I believe. But can I first read the document to see what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, and you can do it out loud so that I don't have to read it out.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was sent from the municipality of Srebrenica to the municipal secretariat for defence in Tuzla. And he says that: "We hereby inform you that 73 women volunteers, assigned to military units of the army of the republic existing in the free areas of Srebrenica municipality, are registered with this municipal secretariat for defence, and three women volunteers are with the Srebrenica MUP. The total number of women volunteers is 76. They are currently assigned to the army and the MUP (units, staffs, institutions) and prior to their assignment to the armed forces, they were not examined by recruiting commission." In the last paragraph, it says: "These women lived and worked in the area of Srebrenica municipality prior to the war. Considering the current situation in the free territory of Srebrenica municipality, we are awaiting further instructions from the Tuzla district secretariat for defence regarding this matter." So he sent this to the district secretariat for defence in Tuzla. Signed by Professor Suljo Hasanovic, secretary. My question is, does this document, sent by Hasanovic to Tuzla, speak to the fact that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had 76 female volunteers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I am really not privy to these details. I don't know. I did tell you that there were some women in the column, but I don't know whether they were soldiers. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are going to see the footage of the column advancing. Can you tell us whether some of those women wore uniforms or parts of uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Probably because they had nothing else to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know any such female members referred to by Mr. Hasanovic out of the 76? Have you ever seen any one of them, given your duties of the military policemen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them worked in the medical unit, but I don't know of any women in the units. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, can you tell us whether in the column you saw a single women? We are going to see the footage. Please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you needn't insist any further. I did tell you that there were some women who also lost their lives in the break-through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any of those women before they were killed as part of the column having worked for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether your questions are directly related to this trial, but it is easy to verify. If there are lists testifying to that, you should bring them here and show them to the Court. It's the easiest thing to do. The army is now a joint force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This Court is well aware of what it is that I can and cannot do. I cannot do what you suggest from where I sit. The Chamber may do that if they find it necessary, but they also have to draw conclusions based on your testimony. If you are not testifying truthfully to this topic, then we can't expect you to tell the truth on other topics. Of course, you are free to answer the way you see fit.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that I replied truthfully and honestly to every question and my only goal is that the truth should out here and that all those guilty should be proportionately sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But please answer my question: Did you see a single woman in that column of whom you learned later that was killed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I did tell you that I did see them, but I don't know whether they were on any army lists. I wasn't placed in such a way to be shown any lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could 1D105 be made part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I note that this was not listed in the list of potential exhibits for your cross-examination. Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm really not familiar with such technicalities, but my legal assistant and I agreed before the weekend that this should be on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. It was an oversight that I am to be blamed for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since there's only one minute left before the break, so as not to start a new topic, perhaps we should take the break now and then start with the topic after that. Thank you. I'd like to thank the witness and everyone else. I would like to apologise again for the overlaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's a good proposal. We have our first break now and we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, I was told that you would like to raise the scheduling issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do. We were just notified this morning by Dr. Haglund, who was currently scheduled to testify this coming Monday, 29 November, that he has had some unexpected heart surgery - he has had something implanted, as I understand it - and he will not be permitted to travel for some time. We still don't have details in terms of what his prognosis or expectation is, for example, to be able to participate, perhaps, in a videolink testimony, which we are exploring scheduling for the end of next week. Again, we are in only the earliest stages of exploring the technical possibilities of that and, just based on prior experience, I would say that they are next to zero, both because it takes a long time technically to set it up, to get Registry on board, and moreover we have a nine-hour time difference between here and Seattle where Dr. Haglund lives, and for a man in his condition to have to get up and get to wherever the videolink would be held from, I just don't see it working. But we are going to explore it because we want to fill as much time as we can and not have any gaps, so we'll explore that. I don't think it's going to be fruitful, so what we'll do next week is we will just move all the witnesses a day earlier, which means we'll have Mr. Mandzic returning for the remainder of his cross-examination, Mr. Razdoljac, who has been subpoenaed by the Trial Chamber, and then Mr. Gavric. If we have any time left over, we'll try to come up with somebody to fill the gap. I can also tell the Trial Chamber, and I believe the Defence wishes to be heard orally with respect to our recent motion to amend the 65 ter list to include numerous exhibits in connection with the Mladic notebooks, we will have Mr. Blaszczyk available, should the court admit his additional exhibits. We'll have him available any time, starting today, although I don't think there will be possibility for him to go today for many reasons, but he will be prepared as soon as the Trial Chamber rules on the motion, I understand that the Defence wishes to be heard on that as well, but that's the brief snap-shot of where the scheduling stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, thank you for this information and the efforts to fill the court time in an appropriate way. One question: Mr. Haglund, if he is not able to testify next Monday, is there another witness available for Monday out of those who are scheduled for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant by moving everybody a day forward was we'll move everybody a day earlier. So Mr. Mandzic will be in place of Mr. Haglund, Mr. Razdoljac will be ready to testify Tuesday the 30th, and Mr. Gavric after Mr. Razdoljac. And if we have a gap after those three that are currently scheduled for next week, we'll find somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me first greet everyone in courtroom. We are sorry about Mr. Haglund not being able to come. We'd like only briefly to state our position regarding the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk. The Defence remains on the same position as represented by Mr. Tolimir; that is, we leave it entirely to the Trial Chamber to decide about the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk and the scope of his evidence. That means the Defence will take no particular position regarding his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this is not the only issue regarding the application by the Prosecution we received this morning. That was in fact a motion to add several documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. What is the position of the Defence to this motion in this respect, and do you want to respond to this motion in written form or orally? What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think there is any need for a written submission. We are concerned about the quantity of material that the Prosecution want to add to their 65 ter list. That is our only concern. As for the rest, that's precisely what I meant when I said we will take no particular position regarding the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk. That includes the extension of the 65 ter list. We leave it entirely to the Trial Chamber to decide on their own conscience about these missions and the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. Then I take it that we can't expect a written response or an oral response to this motion by the Defence and the Chamber will consider the motion of the Prosecution. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber will consider the motion. Nothing else at the moment? In that case, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back, and please sit down. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At the end of the first session we said we would show the Srebrenica video, P991. I would like it to be played because we've already asked certain questions concerning the video, of this witness, and there will be more. P991, please. First of all the forming of the column until minute 14 and then from 33:18 to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear where the video should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you please repeat the end -- the time for the end of the playing of the video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, from 33:18 until 36:46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The video stopped at 35 minutes point 05 seconds. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You saw the beginning when the column was being formed and you heard that man saying, at 11:15:09, "I want to sell this tape to Ramzo [phoen]." Did you recognise that man who said it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, but it's not Ramzo, it's Revda, and her husband is Suad, who is on the list and did not survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. And do you know this man who says, "I want to sell this tape to Revdo," or Revda?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you recognise yourself in this passage that was shown?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Anyone can look for me here, but I'm not there for sure. And if I may add, in the first passage there is a clear indication of time and date, and in the second part at -- there is a point when somebody says, "Just let the people in Pragas be pulled out of there." So that was filmed when we were already emerging at the boundary of the free territory, and you can see exactly how many people had weapons. I even overestimated the number. You can see on this film that one in five or one in six only has a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You must know that we did not edit this. This is a film provided to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence by the Prosecution. We did not tamper with it in any way.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I see there is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see at the beginning, where it says 11 July, 15:09?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it the time when the column began to be formed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat this once again: I am in possession of all my mental faculties and I said in all my statements that on the day when the offensive began I left my house, went down to the centre of town, people were gathering and trying to decide where to go. I don't know where it was filmed because you cannot see any landmarks. This can be in Susnjari or in Srebrenica, and it takes two and a half, three hours of walking to get to Susnjari from Srebrenica. Second, regarding the fall of Srebrenica, Srebrenica definitively fell when the NATO bombed positions around Srebrenica. You can check at what time that was, and that's the time when Srebrenica fell. I watched it all from my house. I was at home at the time, not in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 4 of this transcript today, line 25, the Prosecutor said the column was formed in the night of the 11th July. I am asking you, when was the column formed, considering that the Prosecutor later moved on to questions about Azmir and I don't want to confuse the two topics.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't see the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did the column begin to be formed? Date and time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: My dear sir, I'll repeat to you once again: The forming of the column was spontaneous. Some people left Srebrenica earlier while others were still arriving from peripheral areas. That's how the column was formed, spontaneously and gradually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would again remind both speakers not to overlap. You should pause between question and answer. It's very difficult for the interpreters and for the court record. Secondly, the question was, when was the column beginning to be formed? Despite the -- your answer that was formed spontaneously, but can you give a time estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th, before the final fall of Srebrenica people, were already starting to leave, heading towards Buljim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this film, did you see a part of the column that was filmed during the day of the 11th at 15:09? That's 9 minutes past 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you leave Srebrenica, can you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: After the bombing, when I saw a column of Serbian troops coming into town in a column two by two, I realised that the NATO forces had not done their job. I knew that was it. I locked my home and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand that, but do you remember what time it was? Was it the morning, the afternoon of the 11th?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when the planes bombed the positions of the VRS; in the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember where the VRS assets were at the time when they were bombed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: On the elevations around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: UNPROFOR soldiers testified here that they had looked for tanks as targets on that day, and that they located tanks of the VRS two kilometres far from Srebrenica. Do you know how wide the encirclement was? Were the UNPROFOR positions ahead or behind of the Bosnian army positions around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are asking. We all know very well from which direction the VRS troops came. They passed unhindered by the UNPROFOR soldiers. Nobody stopped them. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if they were stopped by the BH Army in Zeleni Jadar? Did they try to stop them from passing by the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were certain defence lines there. I don't know in which position, but, yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they come in fighting or without any fighting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Most of the time without fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: There was nothing to enable us to give an adequate response. We had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the column leave Srebrenica before the VRS came into the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No. No. The Army of Republika Srpska was pushing the defence of Srebrenica and the population further and further in. They came in from Zeleni Jadar and they pushed the children and women towards Potocari and the men left in another direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We understand that, but did you see any VRS soldiers from the column in which you were at a Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean did I see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If the VRS troops came into the demilitarised zone before you left, did the column see VRS soldiers? Did the VRS soldiers try to stop the column from leaving Srebrenica and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: From Susnjari there is no visibility towards Srebrenica, but they shelled us all the time, hindering our movement. You can really not imagine, dear sir, what kind of feeling that is when they are not letting you leave Srebrenica and they are not letting you live in Srebrenica. That was the only reason why we left; to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That was your reason, but do you know that Srebrenica was a demilitarised zone and that if it had remained demilitarised, if there had been no armed attacks from Srebrenica, it could have remained?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: That's your theory. Just as you say that Muslims killed each other. In Srebrenica it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask e-court to show us D53. While we are waiting, I'd like to say it's a document from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its General Staff, written on the 11th of June, 1995, one month exactly before the Srebrenica events, and it's called "Preparation For Offensives Order." Submitted to the 28th Division of the land forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it now. Preparation for Offensive Combat Operations. It says: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, General Rasim Delic, and in connection with the great success achieved by units of the BH Army ..." et cetera et cetera, "I hereby order: Execute all preparations in the command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of the BH, overextending the A/S and inflicting losses on them, co-ordinating action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the broader Sarajevo area." If you look at this, is it the case that the General Staff from Sarajevo ordered the forces in Srebrenica, including the 28th Division, to prepare for launching an offensive?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Your question is not clear and the text is not clear, because you know that the command and Delic were in Sarajevo, whereas we were in Srebrenica, and I'm probably not even aware of these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the number of this document is not recorded. Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is D53. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the connection between Sarajevo and Srebrenica. It says here Sarajevo, and I was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll show it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D52 to see the connection between this order and Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the screen we see another Army of BH document issued by the command of the 2nd Corps on the 8th of July, 1995. At the time of the events in Srebrenica. It says: "Information on combat results of the units and commands of the 28th Ground Army Division of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." We'll skip the first paragraph. I'll just read out the first two lines of it: "The soldiers of the 28th Land Army Division located in Srebrenica" -- I apologise. "... located in Srebrenica and Zepa, although completely encircled and facing big problems," et cetera, "decided to contribute to the fight," et cetera. In the second paragraph it says: "A number of successful sabotage actions were carried out deep in the temporarily occupied territory where the following results were achieved:" The first bullet point: "60 Chetniks were liquidated and, according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." Then they refer to some seised weaponry. My question is this: Is there a link between Sarajevo and Srebrenica if we look at the activities carried out following the initial order carried out by the soldiers of the 28th Division in the territory controlled by the VRS, whereas they seem to have killed 60 members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I neither can comment or assess -- nor assess these documents. I'm not familiar with these events. I see that there is a certain Suad Delic in the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For your information, the OTP ran their checks and they received this information from your command in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Oh, the Suad Delic of Tuzla. Well, let me tell you this: One should be ashamed to be such a general or brigadier, whatever he was at the time. When we managed to reach Tuzla, he took off his insignia, his rank insignia, and put them in his pocket, he was that ashamed. If this is the Suad Delic that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't know when it is that you saw him. Perhaps you can tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there after the break-through, he greeted us there, but first he took off his rank. I don't know why. Perhaps he was too ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 7 of today's transcript, line 3, you were asked by Mr. Thayer this: "What do you mean when you say that -- that it was taken from TO of OP RS?" And you say the Muslims captured heavy weaponry from Serb positions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I reiterated that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These Muslims who killed the 60 Serbs, were these the people involved?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you seem to be merging two things. At the outset I said that during offensive operations some of it was seised. What you are now saying, that there is a connection between what I said previously and this, I can only tell you that I never heard of this. I don't know about that. I do know that there were incursions and that cattle were stolen, but I'm not familiar with events such as this. If you have a list of killed Serbs, killed on specific dates, perhaps you should show it to us so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will indeed have occasion to see it. Since you are in the witness -- on the witness-stand now, perhaps you can tell us if you know anything about this. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to -- so that we can make sense of the record later, page 43, line 11, General Tolimir appears to be quoting a prior part of the transcript but I'm not sure where that is from because it doesn't look familiar, particularly the reference to "TO of OP RS." I'm not sure anybody has used those acronyms in that way today. So just so that when we go back to the transcript, we know or have a better idea of what Mr. Salkic was answering there so we have a correct understanding of what the question was, I'd like to have that repeated. Or if General Tolimir can tell us exactly where in the transcript or what line that came from, if it's just as easy for him to ask the question again, I don't need a chapter and verse, I just want to know what the question was, but we can't tell, I think, from its current state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it you are referring to page 43, line 14, in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the -- yes, it's line 16 on my screen, but that's -- we are in the same ball-park, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I can be of assistance. I think it is page 8, lines 3 to 5. Occasionally the transcript runs a bit late after Mr. Thayer's question, or Mr. Tolimir's question, and since Mr. Tolimir does not understand the English language, occasionally he notes down a wrong reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help your client to have the right quotation that he can put the question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't need assistance because Mr. Gajic doesn't know what I was about to ask. I put my question regarding examination-in-chief. I think it is page 8, line 3. Mr. Thayer asked: "What do you mean when you say that heavy weapons were seised from the VRS?" This is what I wrote down in shorthand. I don't know what the transcript looked like later on. Then the witness said, on page 8, line 5, the following: "The Muslims captured heavy weaponry from Serb positions." I can now put a new question to the witness because he has already answered this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to have it clear on the record, I would like to quote page 8, line 3. Mr. Thayer is recorded to having said: "Okay. And who was it that seised all of those heavy weapons to begin with?" The answer was: "The soldiers. Muslims seised that weaponry from Serb positions." That is on the record in English. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since I don't speak English, I find this of assistance. I asked the witness whether the same soldiers killed the 60 Serbs in the territory controlled by the VRS, and he provided an answer. If Mr. Thayer would like me to ask that again to receive the answer again, I can only put a new question in relation to the previous one. My question is, or was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
