utterances.text: If that's the question, I would like to receive the response of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only want to say once more that the discussions I had with the investigators about the capturing of heavy weapons, that took place during combat activities prior to the UNPROFOR's arrival. As for this operation or any seising of heavy weapons, that is something I'm not familiar with following UNPROFOR's arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: First of all, I asked you about the combat order sent by the main command of the army from Sarajevo on the 17th of June, and you said that you don't know about that and that you had nothing to do with Sarajevo. Next I quoted to you the order of the corps where the 60 killed Serbs in July were referred to. Perhaps if you want me to tie it all up with Mr. Thayer's questions, then I want to ask you this: Can you tell us whether, before Srebrenica was demilitarised, did you take part in any operations involving the seising of weapons from the VRS, since you spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether your unit participated in the capturing of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Again you put -- you are putting words in my mouth. You say "the unit that you were part of ..." I didn't take any part in any captures or operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps I may have been imprecise.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I think you are doing it on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question and then you can answer. Can you tell us this: Did your unit, the unit that you were in, take part in any capturing of the artillery pieces of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next see D120.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document was issued by the command of the 8th Operational Group in Srebrenica on the 7th of March, 1994. The title of the document is "Supplement For the Guide to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina Chronicle."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 17, please. It's page 23 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The third paragraph begins with "The 1st of May, 1992 ..." It further goes on to say "the enemy was sabotaged in the Zutica sector." It refers to the enemy, which is mentioned in the penultimate sentence of this paragraph. It says, inter alia, that you were also a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. So item 3: "Dates, locations, and brief description of all significant combat activities from the time of establishment until the 31st of January, 1994. On 1 May, 1992, the enemy was sabotaged in the Zutica sector." The unit referring to is the 281st East Bosnian Brigade. What brigade did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I was only a member of Military Police Company. Let me tell you this: If you have lists and rosters, it's no problem to establish anything. There were three Osman Salkic's in Srebrenica in the company I used to work for. It's easy to prove anything, but let me see what people this refers to specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just a moment. This document was received under seal and should not be broadcast, just for the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here that the 281st East Bosnian Light Brigade carried out its attack on 1 May 1992. It was a sabotage operation against the enemy in the sector of Zutica.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Take my word for it, I was never up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, but let me finish reading and then you can tell us whether you participated or not. Then it says: "On 1 May, 1992, enemy sabotage of the command staff at Viogor was avoided." Were you at Viogor on that date?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On 2 May and 3 May, 1992, a strong artillery and infantry Chetnik attack was repelled with the assistance of a group of soldiers from the Potocari TO. Then there are further activities of the unit up until 1993. At the end of this paragraph, it says Visica, or Visnjica in the last line, "On 7 June, 1992, the enemy was successfully" et cetera. There seems to be something missing there. And then we have a number of names. In the third row, it says "Osman Salkic." The cursor is there. It says Osman Salkic. Can you see it? Then it says Mustafa Mujic, Kadrija Mujic, Bekto Memisevic, Sefik Zildic, et cetera. Do you know any of the people on the list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Sir, once again, it's very easy to check the list of military policemen. I don't know any of these persons. If I were afraid of anything, I would ask to be a protected witness, but I'm testifying here in open court. I'm not ashamed of anything or anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm not accusing you of anything, I'm really asking whether you know of any of the people here.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer this question because you were not able to answer this one: You said you were a military policeman. To which unit, according to establishment, did your unit belong?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: We were 20 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's not what I asked. Did you belong to a brigade or a staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I think a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you think you were a staff unit, then we'll go back to the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, let me interrupt you for a moment. At line 15 of this page, 49, there is an indication that the answer was not interpreted I heard in Serbian the answer No, and therefore I would like to put to the witness again. Sir, Mr. Tolimir, asked you, "I'm really asking whether you know any of the people here." What was your answer? And "here" means on the list in front of you. What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll see the document now. A document from the unit to which this witness belonged, he just said they belonged to the staff. It's P957.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While it's being uploaded, I'd like the witness to explain to the Trial Chamber which staff he meant. Is it Naser Oric's staff or the staff of one of the brigades in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: The staff of the command of Srebrenica Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was that inner circle of the command? Where was its location in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: At the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now see this document, again issued by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and since you say at the staff, for the record to be clear, it says command of the operation's group Srebrenica, is that the unit where you were a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: My dear sir, many of your questions are totally confusing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look under 1(a) Lovac, Stari Grad, Srebrenica. Then (b), command of the operative group Srebrenica, up to (e). In which of these bases were you based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: None of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was Naser Oric based, if you were with his staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: At no point did I say that I was with the staff of Naser Oric. Naser Oric had a team of young men who were constantly with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was where was he based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the time the command was at the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where was that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the staff, I said. Although he never sat in an office. He was mostly in the field, on the front lines, visiting troops. He never sat in an office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was the staff located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building from before the war which housed the Territorial Defence staff, and that was kept later by the BH Army for its command. I hope I'm clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this building is located? Where is it situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, as a military policeman, did you ever stand guard, provide security at the building where the staff was based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: To anticipate some of your questions, I'll tell you straight away: I led five or six men in the military police. I was the duty officer in an office and I gave them assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that office in that staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, it was in the old police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How far is that from the staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That old police building, did it belong to the staff and did the police provide security for the staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Honestly, nobody provided security at the staff. There were no guards because only our army was in town. There were these young men around the commander and every unit had someone like a receptionist. People with guns went mostly to the front line and those were people who stayed in town. They knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you said a moment ago that you sat in an office and you gave five men assignments for security missions, did you participate in any of these security missions at the staff? Did you go to the staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I visited the staff, but on no particular assignment. Only if I needed to pass on some information because we had no radio, no communications. And to finish my answer, they did not only on security assignments to the staff, they also went to pass on a message, on another errand, because our police commander lived there. As a military man you probably find this illogical, but in Srebrenica we moved around on foot or on horseback. That's the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand, but I want to know if your unit had any assignments in the staff, or did you go on assignments elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: There was no security for that staff. We were more like a messenger service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, what was the purpose of your unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: In all brigades, I believe there were two military policemen. And anything that happened within a brigade, breach of regulations, would be reported to the military police and then a military policeman would invite the offender for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was your responsibility? Did anyone physically secure the staff? When Naser goes out into the field, he has his own security men, and then you said that people with guns went to the front line. If all the weapons were on the front line, did anyone secure the staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: None of the military policemen did, but there were always people who did some work at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, for the record, what were you doing until 1992, until the mobilisation? To which unit did you belong and what kind of work did you perform?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I was just a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you independent in your work or did somebody give you assignments? Because you said you belonged to the staff.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: We had a military police commander who lived there in the same building, upstairs. He knew everything and he gave us work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: He was an active-duty policeman, a professional policeman. Sakib -- let me remember his last name. He is no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you can give us his last name, and then when we find him we'll find your unit.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I think it might be Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The time it takes us to find him on the list, can you tell us if you knew Naser Oric, the division commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I know him from high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know him from the war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever carry out any assignments, any work in the building where the operations group command was based, where Naser Oric was based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Did I have any assignments there? No, I did not have occasion to do any work for him. He had a team of young men with him that was his permanent entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have no more time to try to establish where you were during the war, I'm giving up on that, because you don't want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is not a correct statement, to say, "you don't want to tell us." The witness has the duty to answer every question here in the courtroom, but some of your questions are not very helpful to assist the witness to answer. If you want to know where the witness was working during the war, I think he told us a lot about that, but I would like to put the question again. Can you tell us where you were during the war? This was the question of Mr. Tolimir, the last one. Can you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the military police in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what else do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have nothing more on the subject because being a member of the military police in Srebrenica is a very broad concept. It gives me no information, but I'm not going on if he doesn't want to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I don't want to, I just don't know what you expect me to tell you. I'm telling you, Naser had an elite team of men that he took with him everywhere. There are many things I didn't like in the war. I chose the military police, in fact, I was assigned to the military police because I had been in the military police in the JNA in the 1985 class, under the command of Captain 1st Class Jeftic. That is why I got assigned to the military police. My philosophy was I only wanted to survive the war. I didn't want to wage war, I didn't want to fight, I just wanted to get out of there alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll come back to my previous question, page 8, line 5, where you said Muslims had seised heavy weaponry from the Serbs on their positions before the demilitarisation. Can you remember where those positions were where the Muslims captured Bosnian Serb weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Where all their lines fell around Srebrenica, on each them, on each of the Serbian lines some weapons were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That means that the BH Army in Srebrenica was the dominant force that could seise weapons from Serbs any time they wanted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Whether it was dominant or not, I don't know, but the fact is they seised some weapons. They had to, because the people in Srebrenica, my dear sir, had nothing to eat. Just like you are trying here to defend yourself in every possible way, that's what we did in Srebrenica. When night falls and you have nothing to give your child to eat, just ask General Morillon what the people who housed him in Srebrenica could give him to eat. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you came to that assignment to General Morillon, did you get that assignment from the division commander staff or from a brigade command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Commander Sakib gave me that assignment, to go there and to see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did that mean that your commander could decide on his own, he didn't have to ask anyone above him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, these were small matters he could decide on his own. Just one more thing I want to tell you: In Srebrenica there was no military regimen like in the Army of the Republika Srpska. When you take a weapon, you never know what the reaction would be, whereas you had order and system in your army. It was very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me go back to your statement. Maybe it will be easier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show -- my legal assistant will give me the number. P1373. Page 3, please. Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The witness should take a look at his own statement, maybe that will help him answer. Thank you. We now have the right page. Paragraph 2 starts with the words: "In the spring of 1992." It says: "In the spring of 1992, I joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is another page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I didn't go to the front line but I did work in the brigade. I provided security to the staff headed by Naser Oric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page is it in English, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 2, the one before this one in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: In your statement you say that you didn't go to the front lines but that you worked within the brigade and secured the headquarters of which Naser Oric was the commander. Can you tell the Chamber what it means when you say that you secured the HQ?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What I said a moment ago: Sakib would send us if something needed to be done. We didn't have standing shifts or duty there. We simply conveyed messages, et cetera. It was sort of logistical support, if someone had to go somewhere, convey a message, et cetera. We weren't providing security for Naser in Srebrenica. There was no one to guard him against. He had a group of his own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those guys and were they members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What guys?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Those who were providing security for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: They were not members of my unit. They were with him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You saw your statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I want to repeat something: I was never with Naser Oric. I never provided security for him. It says here "secured the command," but there was nothing really to secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I simply wanted to quote your statement, and then you can tell us whether it is correct or not. Perhaps it was erroneously noted down. I don't know if that's what you said or not.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine for yourself what sort of tasks I could be assigned to. As I said, sometimes I would be sent to the HQ to convey a message or to bring something, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the second paragraph, the last sentence. You say: "I could hear Serb soldiers over military radio stations, and some of them spoke in Serbian accents." My question is this: Based on what you could hear over the radio, is this what you based your conclusion on about those people speaking with the Serbian accent taking part in the activities around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was in 1992. Let me ask you this: Did you know that in 1992 all Serbs were driven out of certain parts of the Bosnian Croat Federation and that those people came to Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that for a while in the RS the Ekavian dialect was mandatory, it was made mandatory by an Assembly decision, and it was the same dialect that was spoken in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you also know that by virtue of the same Assembly decision, the Cyrillic alphabet or Cyrillic script was made mandatory, as it is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Before the war we were taught both in the Latinic and Cyrillic script. I can understand you very well, whichever language you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know all Serbs who were in the positions around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Of course I couldn't know them all, but there were Serb neighbours who yelled out across the lines. They would say who they were and wanted to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was what you heard over the radio the basis on which you conclude that there were Serbs from Serbia who came to Srebrenica to wage war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at the trial there, I said had there been no Serbia, there wouldn't have been the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this applies to any kind of support, be it in logistics, manpower, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Could the war have been avoided had Bosnia-Herzegovina remained the part of the same state with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you are asking too much. I don't know. It was decided on by the political leadership. Here people are held accountable for the loss of human life, not for political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether there would have been a war if Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to stay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, why would you not honour the will of the Muslim people, then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thayer is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we've travelled this ground already to some degree today. I think the witness has answered consistently when he has been asked essentially the same questions in a slightly reconfigured fashion. Unless there's some new ground that General Tolimir wishes to cover along these lines, I think we've exhausted these very large-scale questions which the witness, frankly, just told General Tolimir is not a matter for his testimony, and frankly, at this stage, with this witness, not fruitful usage of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber always would appreciate if the parties not repeat questions already answered by a witness. And I think this is the case at this moment as well. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I put my questions based on what the witness said. He said that there would not have been the war if the Muslims had been asked, but I asked him whether the Muslims wanted to leave Serbia -- sorry, the FRY where the Serbs lived. That's all I'm asking. He can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this question is already answered by the witness at the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago you said -- you asked me why we didn't defend the referendum held in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm asking you this: Wasn't I supposed, as the soldier, to protect the country that some people wanted to secede from? Wasn't I there to protect its constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is an appropriate question. Who were you defending Yugoslavia from? The Muslim people voted in the referendum, they voted in favour of secession, so why would you not honour that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the SFRY were the Muslims in the majority or the minority, and are you familiar with the procedure applied to any changes of the constitution of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: If I were that familiar with politics, I wouldn't be a worker, I would probably be an Assembly deputy and be much better off in terms of living standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at the outset of the testimony of this witness, we heard about his education and his position as a military police. I'm not sure if this helps your Defence to discuss political questions about secession of a part of the former Yugoslavia with this witness. You should decide to put such questions perhaps to other witnesses. Please focus on those issues the witness can provide answers to you in a sufficient way and carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but he touched upon the problems of the causes of the war. I'm now moving on to paragraph 4 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The fourth line says the dam at Perucac. The witness apparently heard artillery in the environs of the Perucac dam. Was that an important facility for Serbia and Republika Srpska? And was it supposed to defend the dam at Perucac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the reference in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a hydro-electrical plant there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any sabotage operations carried out by any units from Srebrenica aiming at destroying the dam and the plant?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't think it would be so easy to destroy it, although I'm not familiar with whether there were any attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the FRY tasked with defending the dam from any sabotage operations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: If no one was shelling Serbia, why was Serbia shelling Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If Afghanistan did not shell the USA, why did the USA shell Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you should ask that of someone else. Might makes right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's move to page 4 of your statement. In paragraph 2, you say that you worked as part of the security detail for General Morillon when he came to Srebrenica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before that you say that shells landed in Srebrenica from the direction of Ljubovija. It is the first paragraph on page 4.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shells landed the same day when General Morillon was there. Some landed even a hundred metres away from the spot where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask. Were there any ballistics experts present in Srebrenica to ascertain the direction of firing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: That's a ridiculous question, General. You are trying to say again that Muslims were killing Muslims or that UNPROFOR soldiers fired at Morillon? You killed so many people, you should acknowledge that, stand up and say yes, it was us, don't put it on someone else. Just acknowledge that so that we could go on living in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I'm very sorry for that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: ... this is really understandable. On the other hand, it's not a correct statement to say this is a ridiculous question. It is up to the Chamber to decide if a question is appropriate or not. Please, this is the right of Mr. Tolimir to cross-examine you, to put questions to you, and it's better for you to come down a bit, to keep control about your emotions and just answer the questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would that be a good time for the second break so that everybody could come down? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask, we need an accurate estimate from General Tolimir about how much more he has left. We have another witness who is ready to go and we would prefer not to have him waiting around for no reason if there's no realistic chance he is going to start today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you indicate how much more time you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like thank Mr. Thayer for reminding us. We notified that we would use the whole of today's day for this witness, and if you are in no position to grant that, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The time estimation given to the Chamber was slightly different. If I remember correctly, you said two up to three hours, and not the whole day. This is a difference. And therefore I'm very glad that the Prosecution had a reserved witness available today because this is the best way to avoid waste of time. If you need the whole remainder of the -- today's hearing, I think -- do you want to add a something? Do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if my legal assistant promised that we would wrap it up in three hours, I will do so. If there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to make it clear: As the Prosecution, we have no problem with an expanded estimate for cross-examination, we just simply need to know what it is so that we can avoid having the witness sit around. We are perfectly comfortable with going the entire day with the witness. I do have some redirect examination just simply based on some of the documents that were used already, I can tell the Trial Chamber that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, this is always the understanding of the Chamber. It is just a question of your estimation. That's all. You told us you need the whole day and including the examination-in-chief, I think the next witness should be released for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue, let me tell you the following: Mr. Salkic, I know it's the first time that you are giving evidence here in the Tribunal, but please be aware we are in a court, we are in a trial, and have to find out the truth. We are not in a debate on political issues, and we are not in a parliament. And therefore, please think about some of your responses and try to be not too emotional, although after everything you went through, it is understandable. But it doesn't help anybody in the courtroom. I hope you will understand my words. And, Mr. Tolimir, please focus on those areas the witness can provide you with answers as a military policeman and not with -- don't expect too many valid answers on political aspects of this case. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has checked and we have established that so far we have spent one hour and 35 minutes and we have announced that we would need three hours, so we are still within our time-framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 5 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where we see that the witness in paragraph 2 speaks, and that's in the last sentence, where he said: "I went home after various attacks and we were certain that Srebrenica had been captured." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Did all the military and civilian leadership go to Susnjari in this same column that Mr. Thayer spoke about earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had to go via Buljim from Susnjari, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who took the decision for your family to separate and that women go to Potocari and you to Susnjari which happened at Lipjan? Now, you mentioned this in paragraphs 1 through 8.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I took that decision because it concerned my wife, my mother, and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the same true of other families, did the male paterfamilias take the decision?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that mean, since you were the one who took that decision, that part of the military column deliberately left Srebrenica before Srebrenica fell and sent some men, some women and children to UNPROFOR? Is that the decision that was taken by the civilian and military leadership, because they joined you on their way to Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any connection between Susnjari and the central office in Sarajevo? And I'm referring to the military and civilian leadership.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: I'm certain that all communications had been cut before we reached Buljim because I had a radio -- a transistor radio with me. On the second day spent in the woods, I was listening to a news report broadcast by Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina which said that the lines in Srebrenica were holding and they were probably just offering support to other fighters, and of course, I expected that we would get some help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4 of your statement, you say that during the night of the 11th and 12th of July, we formed a column and that you were close to the beginning of the column, together with Muslim men and that this column was about seven kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Who was it who decided that you should be at the beginning of the column?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, no one really made that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who determined how long the column is going to be? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know the details, I don't know who established the column and how that went. Now, you try to figure out when 10.000 to 12.000 people set off from Srebrenica, how long do you think the column should be if they are actually taking the most remote paths?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, maybe I wasn't clear enough in my question. My question actually was this: Was it the civilian or the military authorities who decided that the column should take this remote path through forbidding terrain?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know that, but in view of the fact that Naser and several other platoon and company leaders were -- had been sent for training, I don't know who it was who actually took this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were these people sent to Tuzla for training or did Naser go there on his own initiative, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, you are asking me about several things, but I'll try to be brief. They took him, they took him there, I know, because the helicopter had come to pick him up. Now, had he taken the forest-path, like I did, I would say that he was a traitor of his own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we please see document P67 [as interpreted] to see the reasons why Mr. Oric went to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document to come up, which is D67, in order to save some time, let me say that this is a document that the General Staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 13th of July, which means after the fall of Srebrenica, sent via their 1st Corps through Mustafa Hajrulahovic's commander to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and this document is in fact a report that has to do with some activities involving Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, we can see the document before us, and I would just like to refer you to the fourth paragraph. That's page 2 in English. So bullet point 4 on page 2. I will read it: The preparations for the future operation of linking up the enclaves we brought four brigade commanders and the chief of the 28th Division -- the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, which is Naser Oric. And then it says: The division commander did not return. The division commander, who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight, did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained. Then in the next bullet point it says that there were 17 helicopter flights and each time the helicopter had been hit. Now, this document is familiar to the Trial Chamber because Mr. Thayer asked you in his examination-in-chief whether you knew whether helicopters came to Srebrenica, and you said that they did, so I have no further questions regarding this document, but is it clear to you now that the corps commander -- the corps command and the state command, the army command, actually planned for the linking up of the two enclaves, based on what we read in this document? Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, no, but if I just add, you mention company commanders. Now, I can't really say who the persons were by name, but I know that some of them had gone and then returned. Now, Naser remained there. I don't know why he did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that on the 11th, the night of the 11th, there were negotiations going on in Srebrenica while you were in Susnjari for the refugees to be evacuated from Srebrenica to Kladanj? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have occasion to see on television a video film where -- which shows Mladic negotiating with representatives from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe everyone saw that film.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on that footage, could you see that at the time there were negotiations going on at Fontana Hotel between the civilian authorities in Srebrenica and the army of the VRS -- of Republika Srpska about the evacuation of your family, since you had fled to the woods, and for them to move towards Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe I know more about this than you do. They did negotiate, but the people who had come to the UNPROFOR protected zone, and I believe at that time Naser Mandzic, Muhanovic's father, that was the interpreter, they were the ones who took part in the negotiations. They were already on the base --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, among you, the men, you said 10 to 12.000 men who had left, was it clear to you that there would be any negotiations going on about the evacuation of civilians to Kladanj? Why did you send them off then when you set off? Because I'll remind you of your words: You said that you were the one who took the decision for your family to leave.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, because I expected UNPROFOR to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it also logical, then, for you to expect that there would be negotiations about this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean; about the women and children or about us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I mean primarily the women and children and then we will also touch upon the subject of the men.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, had you, the Army of Republika Srpska, not organised the transport the way you did, probably the UN or the Red Cross or the international community would have intervened and transported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's talk about the military column. Did you in the military column expect that the Army of Republika Srpska would allow you to pass through without -- and you were carrying weapons, to allow you through without any fight, fighting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say, but there were stories going around about exchanges of territories, and I believe you are very well aware of this, and I believe it was a major trap, in fact, because why would so many Muslims actually surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you, but did you expect the military column and, as you said, every third man was armed, did you expect that the Army of Republika Srpska would allow you to go through this territory without any fighting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would have been smarter had they allowed us all to go through, but for fear of having casualties, maybe that's why they didn't do it, so that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Thayer, on page 15 of today's transcript, asked you whether you went through Baljkovica and whether there was any fighting in Baljkovica, and you said yes, 2.500 to 3.000 of us crossed over to the liberated territory. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit more about the fighting there? What kind of fighting was it and what kind of casualties did both sides incur?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't tell you specifically about any casualties and losses. I know that it was pouring with rain immediately preceding our break-through and I know there were already -- it had already been rumoured that the corridor would be open for us to pass through. I believe some tanks were captured, and a Praga and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, who was it who captured these tanks and Pragas? Was it the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Federation army. They captured these weapons on the line along which we were supposed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go through Baljkovica under fighting conditions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Not me, but others have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard in this footage that one person said that Praga and weapons should be taken along.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a reference -- it was from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did the army remove and take away with them the weapons, Praga and other weapons, from Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I went by there, I went through there, but I don't know what happened there exactly, but I know that immediately following that the lines were recaptured again, and what happened specifically, I don't know, but of people who did go there, they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any casualties there, where the Muslim Army was going through the territory in Baljkovica which the Army of Republika Srpska was defending?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I know the men who were killed, but I don't know who was wounded because there were a lot of people there, a lot of our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us any names?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Ejub Golic, one of the commanders, got killed during the break-through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many other people got killed during the break-through?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I can really not give you any figures with any certainty. If I had prepared for this, I could have found some figures on the internet, but I really came here without any preparation on purpose. I wanted to say only what I know. I was overjoyed simply to see that I'm still alive and free. That was where it all ended for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, but you are a witness who went through the column all the way through Srebrenica and participated in the break-through at Baljkovica, as Mr. Thayer asked you. And based on that, I'm asking you, have you seen any Serbian or Muslim losses in Baljkovica or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I gave you one answer, Ejub Golic, I saw him got killed but I didn't see any Serbian casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir be asked to slow down a little and not overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first of all, please slow down and don't overlap. It's very hard for the interpreters and they ask you not to overlap. And secondly, you should switch on your microphone. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said there were about 1.000 rifles. Were there perhaps more?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: You were able to see on your own video how many people carried rifles. That was my rough estimate. We never once lined up and counted how many weapons we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's take, for instance, D126, where Naser Oric says how many weapons there were in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you move to another document, Judge Mindua wants to put a question to the witness in relation to this document on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Tolimir. Witness, we are talking about this column, and you were at the beginning of the column, the head of the column, and you talked about 1.000 rifles, that one person out of three had a weapon. If I understood you correctly, you did not notice any losses on the VRS side. Now, this is my question: While you were in the column I would like to know whether there was any fighting going on. I mean, you were part of the military, so were there any shots being exchanged between the two sides or was this people wandering, you know, at random, with guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was fighting. VRS troops shooting at you and members of the column that were shooting back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see D126. It's a statement made by Mr. Naser Oric which he gave in several instalments to the newspaper Oslobodjenje after the fall in the enclave. We see his photo. I'll read out certain passages and then I'll ask you my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading from the second line of this statement, where it says "Demilitarised Zone." Second paragraph, second line. You know this language, it says: "Demilitarised Zone. At any time of day or night --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At any time of day or night from the beginning of the war until June 1993 when Delic took over, I was in contact with Commander Sefer Halilovic by radio. He was the only man who knew exactly what was going on there. When the order on demilitarisation came, the commander told me to turn over only those weapons which were out of service and useless and heavy guns that we could not hide. That is what we did. We kept defence lines and our weapons." Now, my question is this: After the demilitarisation, were there any weapons on the lines and were Muslim soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Really, I did not walk along the lines and God knows why Naser made this statement. Maybe it was meant as psychological support. When the UNPROFOR came, they came with a list of weapons they needed to receive, that needed to be turned over for them, with numbers and type indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see that list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No, but I know they looked for weapons on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, look at the penultimate paragraph in the fourth column. It says: "Then Zulfo Tursunovic" -- it's page 3 in English. "Then Zulfo Tursunovic and I made a plan and first we cleared Chetnik villages and then we attacked the town and entered the town. Srebrenica was liberated in May 1992 and that was the first town to be liberated in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, my question is, from whom did you liberate Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean "from whom"? The town was held at the outset by Serbs and with a creation of this Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a defence of some sort, and with the assassination of one of the leaders, Goran Zekic, the Serbs left Srebrenica on their own. You can ask why Goran Zekic was liquidated. He was a man who grew up together with Muslims, maybe he was at odds with the leadership of Republika Srpska; I don't know. And there's nothing you can really get from my answer, whatever I answer, because we don't know, we don't have a list of Serbs who were killed in Srebrenica, but there is a list of Muslims, old people, who were buried by the Serbs as they were leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you participate in this liberation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's see the story on the other side. Let's read the last column, where it says: "Guard duty on the line." "Guards along the lines." The last column of the interview, that's it. "We did not want the Chetniks to see the weapons that we had not turned over. That would have given them an argument to refuse to sign the agreement and God knows what else. We certainly had 2.000 rifles that I know about, and I did not know about everything." And then in line 6 -- sorry, line 9, he says: "We left 20 cannons with four barrels which we turned into one-barrel guns. And let me explain, we hid every weapon we captured from the Chetniks and we got them out when we went into action. Everybody hid weapons from everybody. Only the boldest ones, the real soldiers, reported on their weapons. Others hid them until they were needed. It is understandable. So we had probably some 4.000 rifles and it became manifest during the break-through," et cetera. Were you aware that there were weapons inside Srebrenica apart from those that were turned over to the UNPROFOR, less than 200?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were those weapons on the defence lines held by the BH Army around the Srebrenica enclave? Because Mr. Thayer asked you about that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P956.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I'll tell you it's a document from the BH Army, from the command of the 28th Division of Srebrenica, its security section, drafted in June 1995, a month before the fall of the enclave. That's a monthly report, and when you have looked at page 1, it's a document from Srebrenica sent to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to look at the second page, referring to the military police. Page 2. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says, item 4, "The work of the military police." That's where you were. "The military police has been used in keeping with rules and regulations. The military police platoon of the 282nd Brigade has been engaged since 6th June, 1995, on the lines at Ljubosavici [phoen]. Another Military Police Company of the same brigade has been engaged from the 13th to the 22nd June, securing UNPROFOR check-points or observation posts in their zone of responsibility." Were you ever engaged on such duty, securing check-points?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I was in the military police from the -- from -- until 1993. That means that at this date I wasn't with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, if the demilitarisation had been carried out, who would have been in a position to provide security to the UNPROFOR in this month of this year?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I don't know to whom this document was sent. It was maybe just, what they call it, psychological support purposes or maybe to satisfy some military regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim soldiers on those defence lines around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The period relevant to this trial, in July 1995 when there was fighting around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the offensive operations, there were brigades that offered resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where were you then, since you were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber if you had had any duties after 1993 and after the demilitarisation of the UNPA Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No. And even when I got to Tuzla I wasn't involved in anything except I was maybe perhaps recorded on paper, but I wasn't doing anything because I didn't want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that entirely up to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Nobody could force me. I wouldn't have anyone make me do it because the end of the war, for me, was when I got out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But while you were in Srebrenica, could somebody make you go to the lines?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Maybe, but that would have been difficult because there were more volunteers than rifles, plus there was nothing to eat in Srebrenica, and anyone who volunteered to stand guard on the lines at least got one meal a day. Still I didn't want to do it. I stayed at home. But the situation slightly improved when the UNPROFOR arrived. Until the UNPROFOR, there was a different period; you have to distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that after the arrival of the UNPROFOR you managed to receive small amounts of fuel. How was that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, through some channels. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that the UNPROFOR provided you with fuel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, for certain purposes, like the hospital, for generators, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the army receive humanitarian aid and fuel that was meant for the civilians?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how that worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed my cross-examination. We tried to fit in within the time allocated. I thank you, Witness, for your answers. Please don't hold it against me. I have to put to you the questions that I have to. I apologise to the interpreters and the Trial Chamber because of the speed of my questioning and the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful for that, Mr. Tolimir. I would like to put a question to the witness. If I understand you correctly, you left the military police in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we knew that was the end of the war for Srebrenica. I wanted to spend more time with my family. I had obligations towards them because your only source of livelihood was what you could raise in your own vegetable garden, and I had no other option. You can check for the exact date. It was three or four days after the proclamation of the UN protected area. They just told us one fine day there's no more work, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't receive any salary after that time you left the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no salaries in Srebrenica for the army or anyone else. There was nothing for anyone. Only the troops on the lines, in positions, received food, but no money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it your decision to leave the military police or was it a decision by the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My only idea was to survive the war. I felt safer in the military police because we were not exposed to action on the front line. Plus, it was my former duty during my military service in the JNA. That's why they assigned me to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you didn't understand my question. Was it your decision to be demilitarised and to leave the military police? Or was it the decision of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Someone up in the command must have said that the military police was no longer to function, and that's when it all stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe a few MPs remained who did some work for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I'll try to get it done so we don't have to bring Mr. Salkic back. Part of it may be done, I think, outside of his presence; it concerns a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the Presiding Judge's question, Mr. Salkic, did I understand your testimony correctly that the various brigades that were present within the Srebrenica enclave had their own military policemen attached to them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you yourself ever attached to a particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir showed you a document earlier, that's D120, in which he purported to establish that you were a member of the 281st East Bosnia Light Brigade, based in Suceska. Do you recall those questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I do recall the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far Suceska is located from your village of Joseva?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So based on the geographic composition that the 28th Division followed in Srebrenica, would you have had any reason to be part of the 281st East Bosnia Light Brigade which was based in Suceska?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC
utterances.text: I really never belonged to that brigade, but I did say that Salkic was a common last name. I know at least another two people bearing the same name, however, I never was a member of that particular brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have some additional work to do with this particular document. I can tell the Trial Chamber I warned the Defence about using this document for a couple of reasons, but we don't need to do that in the presence of the witness. We can take care of that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have additional questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, on one other topic, but if Your Honour has a question, certainly you'll take precedence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just now in answer to a question from Mr. Thayer, line 15, page 82, he asks you, "And were you yourself ever attached to a particular brigade?" And your answer is, "No." My question for you is: Where were you within the structure of your organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a precise answer. I don't know what unit we exactly belonged to and who were we subordinated to. Believe me when I say that. For example, we never had a single lineup to perform in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How did you come to be in that position? There must have been some call-up or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position do you have in mind? I was assigned to the military police by the secretariat, because they had lists of those who had served in the JNA, with our military specialties. It was for that reason that I was assigned to the tasks of a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Understood. But a military policeman working within which structure? You were not part of a brigade. What were you part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably that of some inner command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think we have to continue tomorrow with re-examination, but I have a follow-up question to Judge Nyambe, the same topic, I would like to put it to the witness. Mr. Thayer asked you: "Did I understand your testimony correctly that the various brigades that were present within the Srebrenica enclave had their own military policemen attached to them?" And your answer was, "Yes." And then the follow-up question was, "And were you yourself ever attached to a particular brigade?" And then you said, "No." I indeed don't understand that. Perhaps we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. What was the reason for that? All of the brigades were based on geographical distribution. One area had one brigade, another area had another, the third had its own. So the brigades were comprised of the local population, and inside each brigade, two or three people were selected to co-ordinate. We, however, were in the town itself and we were a link between the brigade military policemen and the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'll just call the Trial Chamber's attention to page 49 of today's transcript, just for the clarification of this issue and I will have some obvious follow-up questions along this which I think will clarify where the Trial Chamber's questions lie with respect to Mr. Salkic's assignment. I think it's not too complicated or it's not as complicated as it possibly seems at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very sorry, Mr. Salkic, that we have to adjourn for the day. We are over time already. And we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom, and you have to come back again. Be reminded it is not allowed to have contact to either party during the break. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
